title: Class A, B, and C Airspace — Entry Requirements and Equipment

required_knowledge_points.title: Class A Airspace — IFR Only, No VFR, No Exceptions
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Can you fly VFR at FL200?' No. Class A is 18,000 MSL to FL600, IFR only, zero exceptions for Part 91 private pilots. The exam trap: students think a VFR-on-top clearance or Special VFR could get them through it. Neither applies.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class A airspace: FL180 (18,000 feet MSL) and above, up to FL600. Characteristics: (1) IFR ONLY — no VFR operations are permitted regardless of weather conditions. (2) ATC clearance required before entry — a discrete squawk code and ATC two-way radio contact must be established. (3) All aircraft must be IFR-equipped and IFR-rated. (4) Standard altimeter setting: 29.92 in Hg required above 18,000 feet per 14 CFR 91.121. (5) ADS-B Out required under 14 CFR 91.225. No Special VFR, no VFR-on-top, no visual exceptions.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Class A Airspace — Key Facts
- Extends from **FL180 (18,000 feet MSL)** up to **FL600**
- **IFR operations ONLY** — no VFR of any kind, regardless of weather conditions
- No **Special VFR**, no **VFR-on-top**, no exceptions

### Entry Requirements
- **ATC clearance** required before entry
- **Discrete transponder squawk code** assigned by ATC
- **Two-way radio contact** must be established
- Pilot must hold an **instrument rating** and aircraft must be **IFR-equipped**

### Equipment Required
- **Altimeter set to 29.92 in Hg** — all altitudes expressed as Flight Levels (14 CFR 91.121)
- **ADS-B Out** required (14 CFR 91.225)

> **Checkride Trap:** A student who thinks 'clear skies, so I can go VFR above 18,000' is categorically wrong. Class A is IFR-only regardless of VMC conditions

required_knowledge_points.title: Class B Airspace — The Upside-Down Wedding Cake
required_knowledge_points.why: The most common Class B violation: a pilot transitions legally under the shelves but then climbs and unknowingly enters an upper shelf without an ATC clearance. The DPE presents a cross-section and asks: 'At 4,500 feet here — are you in Class B or not?' The answer requires reading the layered shelf structure.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class B surrounds the nation's busiest airports. Structure: tiered shelves ('upside-down wedding cake') — the inner core extends from the surface, outer shelves begin at higher altitudes. Sectional shows ceiling/floor values per shelf (e.g., '60/SFC' = 6,000 ft ceiling, surface floor). Depicted: solid blue lines with altitude brackets. Entry requirements: (1) Explicit ATC clearance ('Cleared into Class Bravo'); (2) Mode C transponder; (3) Two-way radio; (4) ADS-B Out (91.225); (5) Student pilots: CFI endorsement for the specific Class B airport required (14 CFR 61.95). VFR minimums inside Class B: 3 SM, clear of clouds (no cloud separation distances required — ATC provides IFR separation).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Structure
- Surrounds the nation's **busiest airports** (highest IFR operations volume)
- **Tiered shelves** — inner core: surface to ceiling; outer shelves begin at higher altitudes
- Sectional notation example: **'60/SFC'** = shelf from the surface up to 6,000 feet MSL
- Depicted: **solid blue lines** with ceiling/floor altitude brackets

### Entry Requirements
| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| **ATC Clearance** | Explicit verbal clearance — the words **'Cleared into Class Bravo'** must be spoken |
| **Transponder** | Altitude-encoding **Mode C** |
| **Radio** | Two-way radio communication active |
| **ADS-B Out** | Required per **14 CFR 91.225** |
| **Student Pilot** | **CFI endorsement required** for the specific Class B airport — **14 CFR 61.95** |

### VFR Weather Minimums Inside Class B
- **3 SM** visibility
- **Clear of clouds** (no cloud separation distances required)
- ATC provides active IFR separation — the pilot does not need the cloud buffer

> **Checkride Trap:** 'Cleared through Bravo' is NOT the correct clearance — ATC must say 'Cleared **into** Class Bravo' or 'Cleared through Class Bravo airspace'

required_knowledge_points.title: Class C Airspace — The 5 and 10 NM Rings and When the Clock Starts
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'When can you enter the outer ring of Class C without a clearance?' The key: you cannot enter any part of Class C without establishing two-way communication first — but 'N123AB, standby' IS sufficient. No explicit clearance word ('Cleared into Charlie') is needed — only callsign acknowledgment.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class C surrounds airports with FAA radar service. Structure: (1) Inner circle: 5 NM radius, surface to 4,000 AGL. (2) Outer circle: 10 NM radius, 1,200 AGL to 4,000 AGL. (3) Outer area: 20 NM radius — radar sequencing provided, but two-way communication not legally required. Entry requirements (inner/outer circles): (1) Two-way radio communication established before entry. ATC must acknowledge callsign — 'N123AB, standby' = sufficient; 'Aircraft calling, say again' (no callsign) = NOT sufficient. (2) Mode C altitude-encoding transponder. (3) ADS-B Out. No explicit clearance word required. Services provided: radar sequencing, traffic advisories, safety alerts. VFR weather minimums inside Class C: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Class C Structure
| Ring | Radius | Altitude Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Inner circle** | 5 NM | Surface to **4,000 AGL** |
| **Outer circle** | 10 NM | 1,200 AGL to **4,000 AGL** |
| **Outer area** | 20 NM | Radar sequencing provided — no comm legally required |

### Entry Requirements (Inner and Outer Circles)
- **Two-way radio communication** must be **established before entry**
- **Mode C** altitude-encoding transponder
- **ADS-B Out** required
- **No explicit clearance word required** — unlike Class B

### The Communication Test — What Counts?
| ATC Response | Two-Way Comm Established? |
|---|---|
| 'N123AB, standby.' | ✅ **Yes** — callsign acknowledged, may enter |
| 'N123AB, remain outside Class Charlie.' | ✅ Yes — callsign acknowledged |
| 'Aircraft calling, say again.' | ❌ **No** — callsign NOT used; may NOT enter |

### ATC Services Provided
- Radar sequencing, traffic advisories, safety alerts

### VFR Weather Minimums
- **3 SM** visibility, **500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal** cloud separation

required_knowledge_points.title: Mode C Veil and ADS-B Overlap — The 30 NM Rule
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE presents a sectional with a Class B airport and asks: 'At 4,000 feet, 25 NM from the Class B center — what equipment do you need?' Answer: Mode C AND ADS-B Out, even though the aircraft is below any Class B shelf. The Mode C veil and ADS-B requirement extend 30 NM from Class B primary airports regardless of actual airspace class.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Two regulatory boundaries extend beyond Class B airspace shelves: (1) Mode C Veil (14 CFR 91.215): within 30 NM of Class B primary airports, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, an altitude-encoding transponder (Mode C) is required. Applies regardless of whether the aircraft is inside or outside the Class B lateral boundaries — the veil extends beyond the outer shelves. (2) ADS-B Veil (14 CFR 91.225): same 30 NM footprint, surface to 10,000 feet MSL. Aircraft in the Mode C veil but not inside Class B do not need ATC clearance — the equipment requirement is independent of airspace entry.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Mode C Veil and ADS-B Veil — Same Footprint

| Requirement | Regulation | Footprint | Altitude Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode C Transponder** | 14 CFR 91.215 | **30 NM radius** from Class B primary airport | Surface to **10,000 feet MSL** |
| **ADS-B Out** | 14 CFR 91.225 | **30 NM radius** from Class B primary airport | Surface to **10,000 feet MSL** |

### Critical Distinction
- Equipment requirements **apply regardless of which airspace class** the aircraft is actually in
- Aircraft at 8,000 feet, **22 NM** from a Class B airport — **below any Class B shelf** — still **requires Mode C and ADS-B Out**
- **No ATC clearance required** just because of the veil — it is an equipment mandate only

> **Checkride Trap:** The DPE points to a location 25 NM from a Class B airport at 4,000 feet. Correct answer: 'Class E airspace, but Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required because of the 30 NM Mode C/ADS-B veil.' Conflating 'not in Class B' with 'no Mode C needed' is a known oral exam failure point

lesson_overview:
## Class A, B, and C Airspace — Entry Requirements, Equipment, and the Busiest Sky in America

Imagine you're planning a flight that takes you through the Charlotte airspace and then above FL180 enroute to the northeast. That route crosses three different airspace classes — each with different entry rules, different equipment requirements, and different pilot certificate requirements. Getting any of these wrong is not just a checkride failure — during a real flight, it's an airspace violation, potentially an intercept, and a FAR violation that doesn't disappear.

**Class A: IFR only, no exceptions.** Class A begins at FL180 and extends to FL600. No VFR operations of any kind — no Special VFR, no VFR-on-top, no exceptions for clear conditions. If you're in Class A, you have an IFR clearance with a discrete squawk code. Above 18,000, the standard altimeter setting is 29.92 in Hg. ADS-B Out required.

**Class B: the upside-down wedding cake.** Class B surrounds the nation's busiest airports. The geometry: tiered shelves with the inner core at the surface and outer shelves beginning at progressively higher altitudes. Getting to the airport doesn't mean you're in Class B — you may be legally below a shelf. Entry requires explicit ATC clearance, Mode C, ADS-B Out. Student pilot restriction: cannot enter specific Class B without CFI endorsement. The weather minimum inside Class B is unique: 3 SM and clear of clouds — ATC is separating you from all IFR traffic.

**The Mode C Veil: the 30 NM gotcha.** Even if you're below any Class B shelf — say, 25 NM out at 4,500 feet — if you're within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, you need Mode C and ADS-B Out. This is independent of airspace class. Equipment mandatory regardless of which airspace you're actually in.

**Class C: the 5 and 10 NM rings.** Class C surrounds airports with FAA radar service. The inner ring (5 NM, surface to 4,000 AGL) and outer ring (10 NM, 1,200 to 4,000 AGL) both require two-way communication established before entry. ATC must acknowledge your callsign — 'N123AB, standby' is sufficient. 'Aircraft calling, say again' without your callsign is not. No explicit clearance word ('Cleared into Class Charlie') is required — just callsign acknowledgment.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE points to a sectional at a location 25 NM from a Class B airport at 4,000 feet. The question: 'What equipment do you need and what airspace are you in?' If below the outer Class B shelf, the answer might be: 'Class E airspace, but Mode C and ADS-B Out are required because of the 30 NM veil.' Students who conflate 'not in Class B' with 'no Mode C needed' fail this on the spot.
